sections.html:
Shoreline sits on Seattle's northern edge in the northwest corner of King County, and most homes here are lived in by their owners (66.3 percent). The July 1, 2025 estimate is 66,542 residents, a 13.8 percent gain over the 2020 base. Turnover is modest: 88.3 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier.

Many residents commute to Seattle, averaging 27.2 minutes each way. Two Link light rail stations beside Interstate 5, Shoreline South/148th and Shoreline North/185th, give nearby streets an easy selling point, so name the closer one in your listing.

Shoreline is split into 14 neighborhoods, with Richmond Beach in the northwest corner, and The Highlands is a gated community that has its own sewer district. Does your street have special rules or a homeowners' association? Say so up front. The state disclosure form asks about association assessments, common areas and approvals needed for remodeling, and buyers prefer to hear it from you.

If an association applies, request its governing documents, dues schedule and any notice of upcoming assessments as soon as you decide to sell. Associations can take days to answer, and a buyer's review period runs on a clock.

Shoreline treats a missing permit as a violation that stays with the property. Starting work without one breaks city code and can mean fines and penalties, with permit fees possibly doubled. The current owner answers for what earlier owners skipped, so check the record before you list.

The city sorts everyday jobs roughly like this:

  • Cabinet replacement, painting and tiling usually need no permit, unless plumbing, electrical or gas work comes with them.
  • Moving a wall, door or window probably needs a building permit. So does swapping a water heater or adding a permanently wired light fixture.
  • Plumbing and mechanical permits can sometimes be issued the same day. Other reviews take longer, depending on project type and how complete the documents are.
  • Applications go through the city's eTRAKiT system, where anyone can check a permit's status without an account. Send questions to pcd@shorelinewa.gov.
  • When work started without a permit, the city can require a separate investigation inspection permit before it will take the building permit application.

Look at trees as well. A tree that poses an imminent hazard can come down under the municipal code, but a healthy tree with only moderate risk may still need a permit, and cutting one without a permit can draw penalties sometimes reaching $15,000 or more.

A quick way to start: walk the house with a list of every project since you bought it, then email the city with addresses and descriptions of anything doubtful. Keep the replies with your sale papers.

Buyers' agents often ask who serves an address, because several providers split the work.

  • Electric: Seattle City Light covers every property in the city.
  • Water: either Seattle Public Utilities or North City Water District, depending on the address, as the city's property information map shows.
  • Trash, recycling and compost: Recology.
  • Natural gas: Puget Sound Energy.

Wastewater is handled by the city everywhere but The Highlands. Two treatment plants serve Shoreline, one operated by Edmonds and one by King County, and a layer on the city's managed assets viewer shows where a given parcel drains. The disclosure form asks if the property is on public sewer, whether the house is hooked up, and whether extra sewer charges apply, so verify each answer with the city before you sign.

sections.h2: Closing costs and the disclosure form
sections.html:
Excise tax on the sale is the largest closing cost, and the seller is the normal payer. If the seller leaves it unpaid, the buyer becomes liable and the unpaid amount may become a lien. Tiers are 1.1 percent up to $525,000, 1.28 percent from there to $1,525,000, then 2.75 percent and 3 percent in the higher bands. For sales starting January 1, 2027 the breaks sit at $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. The local rate comes on top.

Call the King County treasurer for the Shoreline rate and the property tax balance on your parcel, and ask escrow how the year's tax will be split.

Expect to deliver the disclosure statement within five business days after both sides accept a written contract. From delivery, the buyer has three business days to rescind, unless that right was waived. The form also has you confirm that carbon monoxide alarms and smoke detection are in place.

sections.h2: From accepted offer to closing day
sections.html:
Knowing the order of events helps you plan a move. After you and a buyer sign a written contract, the clock starts on your disclosure statement, due within five business days. The buyer then reads it and, within three business days of delivery, may rescind unless the right was waived.

While that window runs, title work goes on in the background. The title company looks for liens and unpaid taxes, asks for your loan payoff figure, and prepares the deed. If the file shows unpermitted work or an unclear sewer connection, expect questions, and have your answers ready from the permit emails and city records you collected.

On closing day you sign the deed before a notary. The notarized date is the sale date for excise tax, and the tax and affidavit go to the county. Funds reach you once the deed is recorded. If you are moving out, plan your last day in the house around that date, and keep copies of utility final bills for Seattle City Light and your water provider, since the buyer will want service transferred.

When the house needs more work than you want to take on, a cash buyer who accepts it as-is is the alternative to listing. Weigh any offer against what a repaired and listed sale would leave you after repairs and carrying costs.

Both routes need the same folder: the deed, a loan payoff figure, permit records for work you or earlier owners did, and your latest property tax statement. In a cash sale, escrow opens once you accept and the title company searches the record. The loan is paid from proceeds, you sign the deed in front of a notary, and the county receives the excise tax and affidavit. Funds are released after recording. No appraisal or lender review slows things down.

faqs.q: How many people live in Shoreline, WA?
faqs.a: The July 1, 2025 estimate is 66,542. The 2020 census counted 58,608, a gain of about 13.8 percent.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel a Shoreline house before I sell it?
faqs.a: It depends on the work. Painting, tiling and replacing cabinets generally need no permit, but moving walls, doors or windows likely does, as does replacing a water heater. Email pcd@shorelinewa.gov with a description if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Am I responsible for unpermitted work a previous owner did?
faqs.a: Yes, the owner answers for earlier unpermitted work. The city may ask for an investigation inspection permit before it accepts the building permit, and fees can be doubled.

faqs.q: Can I remove a tree from my Shoreline lot before listing?
faqs.a: Only if the rules allow it. A tree that is an imminent hazard can be removed, and dead or dying trees outside critical areas have exemptions, but healthy trees may need a permit. Penalties for removing one without a permit can reach $15,000 or more.

faqs.q: Who supplies electricity and water in Shoreline?
faqs.a: Seattle City Light provides electricity citywide. Water comes from Seattle Public Utilities or North City Water District, depending on the address. Puget Sound Energy supplies gas, and Recology picks up trash, recycling and compost.
